clinicalPearls: A primary lymphocytic cicatricial alopecia representing follicular involvement by lichen planus, typically affecting the vertex and crown with patchy scarring
Perifollicular erythema and follicular hyperkeratosis, with tubular scale hugging the emerging hair, are characteristic at the margins of expanding bald patches
Patients may report itching, burning, tenderness or trichodynia over the affected scalp
Loss of follicular ostia within the patches confirms scarring, and several small patches may coalesce into larger areas
The Graham-Little-Piccardi-Lassueur syndrome combines scalp scarring alopecia, non-scarring loss of axillary and pubic hair, and follicular keratotic papules on the body
It may be associated with lichen planus of the skin, nails or mucosae, and frontal fibrosing alopecia is regarded as a clinical variant
Treatment targets the inflammation with potent topical, intralesional or systemic anti-inflammatory therapy to arrest progression, since scarred areas will not regrow
reference.pathophysiology: Lichen planopilaris is a T-cell-mediated inflammatory disorder in which a lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate targets the follicular epithelium, particularly the bulge region housing the follicular stem cells. Destruction of these stem cells and of the sebaceous glands leads to permanent follicular loss with perifollicular fibrosis. It is considered a follicular expression of lichen planus, and loss of follicular immune privilege as well as altered peroxisome-proliferator-activated receptor signalling have been implicated, but the end result is irreversible cicatricial alopecia.
additionalDifferentials: Discoid lupus erythematosus, with scaling, dyspigmentation and follicular plugging
Frontal fibrosing alopecia, a clinical variant affecting the hairline and eyebrows
Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia, centred on the crown in afro-textured hair
Folliculitis decalvans, which is neutrophilic with pustules and tufting
Pseudopelade of Brocq or other end-stage scarring alopecia
additionalInvestigations: Trichoscopy showing perifollicular erythema, tubular scaling and loss of ostia
Scalp biopsy from an active margin demonstrating lichenoid perifollicular inflammation and fibrosis
Direct immunofluorescence to help distinguish it from discoid lupus
Examination of skin, nails and mucosae for coexisting lichen planus
Disease-activity assessment to guide and monitor treatment intensity
redFlags: Rapidly expanding or highly symptomatic patches indicating active disease and impending permanent loss
Features overlapping with discoid lupus that require different systemic management
Extensive multifocal scarring threatening widespread irreversible alopecia
reference.prognosis: Lichen planopilaris follows a chronic, unpredictable course; treatment can reduce symptoms and slow progression but cannot regrow hair in scarred areas, and disease may reactivate after periods of quiescence.
pitfalls: Failing to biopsy an active margin and so missing a treatable inflammatory scarring alopecia
Confusing it with discoid lupus, which differs in management and immunofluorescence
Sampling a burnt-out scarred centre rather than the active edge on biopsy
Underestimating the symptom burden of itch and pain that should guide treatment intensity
management: Apply potent or superpotent topical corticosteroids and give intralesional corticosteroid injections to active margins to suppress perifollicular inflammation
Use topical calcineurin inhibitors as a steroid-sparing anti-inflammatory adjunct
Start systemic hydroxychloroquine as first-line oral therapy for progressive disease

Escalate to oral retinoids, ciclosporin, methotrexate or mycophenolate mofetil, or a short course of systemic corticosteroids for rapidly advancing scarring, with pioglitazone (PPAR-gamma agonist) as a further option
Control symptoms of itch, burning and trichodynia
Monitor progression with serial trichoscopy and disease-activity scoring, recognising that hair cannot regrow in scarred areas
Offer camouflage, wigs and psychological support for the alopecia
Refer to dermatology or trichology and examine skin, nails and mucosae for associated lichen planus and frontal fibrosing alopecia
